stem: Box A contains 3 cards numbered 1, 2 and 3. Box B contains 2 cards numbered 1 and 2. One card is removed at random from each box. Build the sample space: tap every outcome (card from Box A, card from Box B) that could happen.
solution: An outcome records the card from Box A first and the card from Box B second, as an ordered pair $(a, b)$.
Any card from Box A can come out together with either card from Box B, so go through Box A one card at a time.
Box A card 1 gives $(1, 1)$ and $(1, 2)$; card 2 gives $(2, 1)$ and $(2, 2)$; card 3 gives $(3, 1)$ and $(3, 2)$.
An event such as "the sum is 4" is only a part of this set, $\{(2, 2), (3, 1)\}$. It is picked out of the sample space; it is not the sample space itself.
notes: The sample space of a one-from-each-box experiment is exactly the set of ordered pairs A x B, so this is the objective's "identify the sample space" half, built outcome by outcome; it is the first step the book's question ex14-8-22 needs before any event can be picked. missing-pairs is mapped to sample-space-as-an-event: the likeliest reason a student leaves out cells when asked for every possible outcome is that they list only the pairs for the event the problem is about (sum 4, product at least 3). It will also fire for plain carelessness, which this predicate cannot tell apart. reversed-pairs (Y x X) is unmapped: none of this objective's own misconceptions describes it. sample-space-of-another-experiment cannot be diagnosed here because extra-pairs is not among the predicates this widget reports. Sets are kept to 3 and 2 numbers, inside the instrument's limits.
